maintopic: STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER RESPECTING SECURITY PRECAUTIONS

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER RESPECTING SECURITY PRECAUTIONS
speechtext:
Following yesterday's disturbing occurrence many hon. members have raised with me the question of security in the parliament buildings. I believe that generally speaking the security precautions enforced in this building over the years have been entirely adequate.
As hon. members know, it is not easy to reconcile the enforcement of strict security regulations with the degree of freedom of access to the building and the galleries that the Canadian people have come to expect when visiting parliament. We must strive to achieve a reasonable balance between these two requirements of security on the one hand and public interest in the affairs of parliament on the other hand.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
I will not suggest that the arrangements currently in force are perfect. It is quite possible that improvements could be achieved in some way without undue inconvenience to the visiting public. With this in mind the whole subject of security will be reviewed forthwith, and suggestions proferred by hon. members or by anyone interested in the matter will receive every possible consideration.

maintopic: STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER RESPECTING SECURITY PRECAUTIONS
speechtext:
Hear, hear.

May I also pay a tribute to the sergeant-at-arms and the members of the security staff of the house. Too often we take for granted the devotion to duty of those employees. Yesterday, under extremely distressing and difficult circumstances, those employees proved their good judgment, their self-control and efficiency to an extent which honours them and justifies the confidence we place in them.

speechtext:

MR. HOWARD-ARTICLE IN OTTAWA "JOURNAL" OF MAY 18
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege which affects me and undoubtedly affects others as well. My question of privilege relates to an article in the Ottawa Journal of yesterday, May 18, written by Peter Jackson. The lead sentence may receive some modicum of support, because it starts by saying "Shame on you, Frank Howard!"
I might say that my question of privilege does not have to do with that first sentence. It has to do with the tenor of the article which quotes part of an editorial in the Omineca Herald, which is a weekly newspaper in my home town and constituency of Terrace and Skeena. The article relates to the Ottawa city streets, curbs, gutters and so on, and draws a comparison between the condition of the streets in my home town of Terrace as enumerated in this editorial, and the condition of the streets here in Ottawa. It says in effect, shame on me and undoubtedly on others who have similar conditions in their home towns and who have raised the matter of the deplorable condition of Ottawa streets.
I should like to say to the writer of the article, and any others, that they have grossly misunderstood and misinterpreted the whole concept of what we are trying to get at. I can assure hon. members that if they desire to move the capital of Canada to the community of Terrace, we will be overjoyed and you will have the most delightful street system in Canada there.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. HOWARD-ARTICLE IN OTTAWA "JOURNAL" OF MAY 18
speechtext: There is no prima facie case of privilege. The one thing the hon. member might have complained of-the words "Shame on you, Frank Howard"-was not complained of by the hon. member, so I rule there is no question of privilege.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman has put several questions. The hon. member for Halifax also put a question which is closely related, I think, to some of the matters raised by the hon. member for Queens.
The position taken by the federal government and the position, if I understand it correctly, of the government of Newfoundland is that the McNair award under term 29 should be assimilated to the constitutional subsidies provided to other provinces in the original act of confederation, as amended from time to time, and to the subsidies provided in the terms of union with the other provinces which subsequently came into confederation. The award should not be confused with tax-sharing or equalization.
It is true that the monetary award of $8 million was incorporated as part of the taxsharing legislation of the previous government, and from the monetary standpoint this bill will make no difference. What it does is to make provision of this kind permanent unless at some time the parliament of Canada decides to repeal this act. In other words, it puts the matter in a different position.
It is true, as the hon. member for Carleton suggested, that we might have proposed an address to the British parliament and asked them to incorporate this provision in the British North America Act. If the government of Newfoundland had felt very strongly about it, then perhaps that would have been a course which might have commended itself to the whole of parliament. That was done, of course, with the original terms of union and it was done with the terms of union of most of the other provinces.
However, the government of Newfoundland indicated that they would accept the good faith of the parliament of Canada. They agreed that, if it was done in this way, no parliament would ever change it unless there was agreement between the then government of Newfoundland and the government of Canada that it should be changed. I think it is fair to say that they have taken the view which the present federal government takes

and which the leader of the government took when he was on the other side of the house and has taken consistently, namely, that this should be done as part of the terms of union and done on the same kind of basis as the other parts of the terms of union, as completion of the constitutional subsidy of Newfoundland.
In many ways, Mr. Chairman, this course is very comparable to something with which the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton is very familiar, namely, the awards of the White commission which were made in the thirties and which were not incorporated as an amendment to the British North America Act but were made a statute of this parliament. Those sums have been paid to the three maritime provinces annually ever since.
I am sure that any proposition that these subsidies be taken away unilaterally by this parliament would be defeated by this parliament. I am sure the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton would agree with that view. Therefore it is felt by us, and after the vote we have just had I am more reassured, that this act will adequately complete confederation.
If the McNair commission had seen fit to recommend that this amount be revised from time to time according to some formula to take account of changing factors, then, since most Newfoundlanders would feel that it would probably be revised upwards or not at all, they would have been very happy. There was not too much satisfaction expressed in Newfoundland when the award was first made. But the McNair commission did not recommend that course; they recommended a fixed sum.

Mr. Chairman, as we take part in this debate it is important, to recognize the significance of what the minister is
May 19, 1966

Vocational and Technical Training
proposing. It was a significance which goes beyond the bare announcement made by the hon. gentleman. We are encouraged to believe there is a new understanding of manpower, as evidenced by the reconstruction of the department and the appointment of the present minister. It is most heartening to read a statement by the hon. gentleman recently expressing his belief that this problem cannot be solved unless the community as a whole takes a new attitude toward the importance of training and comes to regard training as a normal and productive part of people's lives, as something that should be equated with work rather than with unemployment and welfare.
This represents a great departure from the practice in the past and I am sure there is not a member in the house who will not applaud this new approach. I should like to join with the hon. member who has just resumed his seat in the suggestion that we adhere to this principle and see that the equating of work with training is carried to its logical conclusion by making $1.25 the minimum basis of payment. If we are to honour the minister's statement with the full force of the law I think we should seriously consider making the initial payment greater than $35.00 so that it will be more in line with the labour code now on the statute books. The minister might wish to make some adjustments with regard to the other levels. But he has postulated an important principle and perhaps he needs to take action to ensure that this principle is fully understood and that we have a total commitment to it.
I should like to quote now from a publication entitled "Technical and Vocational Education in Canada". The following is an extract from the speech by Mr. W. R. Cranston, chairman of the Ontario Economic Council, illustrating what I call the new attitude toward manpower:
The days of the big "gold rushes" in terms of available and exploitable human and material resources in this country may well be coming to an end. We must now, to hold our place in this world, examine our manpower and natural assets in much greater detail and provide an economic and educational climate in which their contribution to our national and international growth can and will be more readily maximized.
While I am on this subject I should like to compliment the Department of Citizenship and Immigration together with the director and editor of this magazine. I think this is a most worthy effort and it contains excellent information on the whole subject of manpower.


It is fairly obvious that the provisions contemplated in this resolution are overdue. From personal experience, as well as from the experience of others who are familiar with this subject, I believe that the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act should not be used as a means of paying those who are engaged in training.
First of all, as I think the minister pointed out, the man who took a course of training for a considerable period of time was often placed at a serious disadvantage. If he became unemployed at what I might perhaps call the wrong time of the year, his right to insurance payments was forfeited and as a result he was penalized because of his effort to train. The recognition that unemployment insurance should not be related to training is laudable. The one has nothing to do with the other. A man's insurance rights should remain open to him in case he has need to call on them. But for the efforts of some very dedicated people who were working on program five I think the program would have been even more disastrous than events have proved.

I point out these things to indicate the great need that has existed for the kind of measures the minister has introduced. In my riding we went into program five at a very early date. One of the aldermen on council, Mrs. Donaldson, took a keen interest and she was ably assisted by Mr. Rice who headed up the program and had an excellent staff. They are really dedicated people. They have to be. They are not only trying to make program five work but they have to be social workers as well because part of the payment is made under the Unemployment Insurance Act and part is made by the province.
Sometimes one cheque or the other would not come through. Frequently there was no relationship between the two, and the amounts were small enough without people being deprived of the payments at the time they needed them. There were other problems besides money in trying to keep people at school, but money was an important problem. Living on a day to day basis without funds to fall back on meant that the only way they could stay in school was to receive their payments at the proper time.
Whenever there was a technical hitch, a departmental error or conflict between the two agencies, this made the whole problem more difficult. In fact, some of the teachers

had to dig into their own pockets and advance loans to pupils in order to keep them at school. Should we expect our teachers to be performing this function? Obviously the government now feels that this is not the function of the teachers.
We have a program which is quite good but it is important to recognize that we have dedicated people in the teaching profession who have kept an inadequate program going for a long time and deserve our commendation.
I would also like to point out the difficulty with regard to the excellent program in the city of Kitchener at Waterloo Collegiate. The program is headed by Mr. Charles Rushton and I am pleased to see that the government has recognized the abilities of this man by promoting him to a higher position. An article in the Kitchener-Waterloo Record of last February deals with a $100 gift by the local I.O.D.E. chapter to program five but to Mr. Rushton in particular so that he would have some kind of kitty to help people in training stay at school. Among the problems he had to cope with were a deserted mother who needed funds to buy baby food, streetcar tickets for 20 people for ten days, aiding three women from northern Ontario to get suitable accommodation, aiding a Cape Croker Indian boy who needed clothing and accommodation, and issuing cafeteria tickets to numerous people ensuring them of at least one hot meal a day.
The record indicates that less than half of the people who enter program five complete the course. It is difficult to know just how many of them drop out because of lack of funds but there is every indication that a fair number of them are in that position.
I submit that no country needs education, and inducements toward that end, more than Canada. We are a small country with a limited population but we have a huge area of land. We cannot do some of the things that other nations with massive populations can accomplish. The implication of all this is that if we are to have any future at all it is as a nation of quality, and to achieve quality we have to place great emphasis on training, retraining and the education of our people.
We need a highly trained and skilled work force. It has often been said that this country was founded by a group of French and English people who were proud husbanders and tillers of the soil. That was true at a time when 70 to 80 per cent of the population was

But with the increase in factories and industrialization which has taken place, many people have had to leave the farms and come into cities. Frequently they have been poorly equipped for the new challenges facing them. For many it meant a loss of respect and a sense of dignity, the kind of dignity that comes from knowing one's occupation is important and that one can rely on one's hands to perform the tasks set for them. A lot of this has been lost as a result of the shift from a rural to an urban population, and there is a great need for education if for no other reason than to restore a sense of pride in our work force. I would ask the minister to give serious consideration to the way that the money is allocated to the various provinces. Admittedly the federal grants of 90 per cent and 75 per cent on capital construction are fairly substantial. They are fine for those provinces that retain the work forces they train, but it is not a good proposition for many provinces that are merely training their people for migration to other provinces. This is a problem which the minister should consider to see if he can devise a formula based on immigration or emigration province-wise. It is frequently the poorer provinces which find themselves in this position. It is unfair to say to a province that here is a training program which is going to increase the abilities of its people when frequently it also means it increases the mobility of its trained people so that they can move to greener pastures. It is unfair to ask the poorer provinces to carry this burden. This is a national problem. Vocational and Technical Training
I believe it is in order to insist on this special aspect of the resolution, since certain changes incidental to this program must also be provided in connection with the administration of the Unemployment Insurance Act.
Nobody will be surprised if I add that the Unemployment Insurance Act, passed more than 20 years ago, is still not perfectly understood by all contributors, employers, employees and a large percentage of officials. The reason is that the drafting of many clauses is so complicated that it allows various interpretations in the minds of certain officials who are not sufficiently aware of working conditions, and who may influence the worker accepting a job or leaving his place of employment.
The official concerned often makes prejudicial decisions because he is usually inclined to accept the employer's account of the facts instead of trying to clarify the situation by taking also into account the employee's explanations.
True social legislation bearing the name of unemployment insurance must protect the unemployed at least as much as the fund. Unfortunately, the opposite is often true and the fund is better protected than the unemployed.
I wished to point out that fact since the resolution deals with allowances which, in some cases, will adjust benefits paid to the unemployed who are ready to take courses.
Many were having difficulties last winter with regard to this, for example because of delay in checking the files, which determines eligibility for allowances, or in the payment of adjustment allowances; as a result, some of the unemployed had to borrow money to continue their courses and others received a ridiculous allowance adjustment.
I have a cheque here for 40 cents, which is not even enough to buy a light meal. Others, living near the school, received a regular weekly allowance of $10 to $12, as compared to those living some miles away and even in neighbouring parishes who received the same or a smaller amount, while a great many received nothing at all. An unemployed married man with dependant children cannot pay his transportation to school with his benefits; he must use the latter to provide for his family, which is normal. Automation has clearly forced the young and the not so young, who would once have

part relating to amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. There are many people who are not covered by unemployment insurance. I think particularly of farm labourers and hospital employees who could easily be covered and should be entitled to coverage.

It is a reform measure in that the minister recognizes that the present vocational training program is not working but the need for training is there. But as soon as he goes to the vocational training school and sees the blackboards, the teachers .and all the formal parts of education he becomes rather apprehensive. I put it to the minister that in this instance we do involve the federal government, the provincial governments and the individual, but we fail to involve the most important group and that is management. The ordinary working man or tradesman, after 10 or 12 years in a shop, becomes involved with the people who are there as supervisors, the union labour group. It would be much better if some provision could be made by which he could take retraining while he is still involved with this group instead of being cut

DEBATES	May 19. 1966
off separately as an individual who has to try to make it on his own with all these apprehensions and all these fears.
I recommend to the minister that he consider whether a payment of up to $80 or $90 could be made directly to the employer who in turn could add to that. After all, the employer is going to get the benefit of the man's retraining. If this were done, the workmen's pay would not be so drastically reduced. In addition management, labour and government would be involved in one project concerning one person's future.
There are difficulties with this scheme, of course. However, we must remember that automation is one of the greatest worries of labour, management and government today. This may be one method by which a start could be made toward the solution of the problems facing us as a result of automation. Provision could be made under which the employer, if he so desired, might continue to keep the workman on his payroll and at the same time get the benefit of the money the government would pay. I presume the employer would still have to contribute money of his own but I do not believe he would mind doing that. He would have the benefit of that person's training within his own organization in the future.
Labour unions could also be involved in this scheme with the result that-and this is most important-the workman would still be within the organization to which he has contributed for 10 or 15 years and which he recognizes as his group. He would derive a lot more encouragement to continue his retraining and thus achieve one of the purposes of this resolution.

I think there may be many people disillusioned with the members of this parliament. However, I believe we have a large number of good members and there is a lot of talent among the new members. I say to the
May 19, 1966	COMMONS
minister in this house, as I have told him privately outside, that he has made a splendid contribution in the cabinet and in the house. He is to be congratulated for his refreshing point of view and his candour. One hopes that he will spread it to his colleagues and will not suffer from a malaise emanating from them. The minister has broken away from the gate and is one of the leaders of the new talent in this chamber.
One of the attractive aspects of the resolution is the provision for the training of those who were self-employed but who were having difficulty in such primary industries as farming, fishing or logging. People have been caught in these primary industries without being able to make a go of it on their own and yet they really are fastened to their fishing communities or their small farms because there is no alternative. I should like to make two points, sir, with regard to what I call safeguards because, after all, we are dealing with public money. Therefore I suggest these points to the minister.
The minister has referred to training for the unemployed. Mr. Chairman, one of the difficulties in being so far down the roster of speakers is that most of one's thoughts have already been expressed by other members when one's turn is reached, so I will be brief.
I join with the hon. member for Halifax in his eulogy of the minister. It seems to me an incredible oversight on our part not to have drawn this fact to the attention of the house. Perhaps we felt it so self-evident that it did not need to be drawn to the attention of the house. We are equally proud of his achievements, particularly as a freshman minister, which must be infinitely more difficult than just being a freshman member.
The resolution before us is to my mind one of the more interesting and exciting resolutions we have seen in the house this session. It seems there is almost the possibility that we are moving into a sort of age of enlightenment when it comes to industrial relations. If the initiative is being taken by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, more power to him. Too often in the past human considerations have been missing in a general assessment of the problems in an age of technology and it is imperative that this dimension be introduced into our thinking. I think Mr. Justice Freedman made an important contribution along this line and I hope that both his principles and philosophy are reflected in future government legislation no matter which party happens to be In power, as well as in the attitude of management.
It has been my experience, albeit brief, that the major and paramount preoccupation of industrial workers is concern for job security. At the same time industry is in the grip of technological innovation. If this country and its industry are to compete in world markets, and it is imperative that we do so, then in turn we must watch very closely the level of productivity. We must capitalize on technological developments, and recognize the necessity for constantly automating the processes of production. However, job securitj
5310	COMMONS
Vocational and Technical Training and technological innovation are mutually contradictory. Job security is an almost impossible goal, or would appear to be, in an age of wide ranging change. There is no possibility of changing the need for technological innovation; it is a fact of life, and automation is a by-product of this innovation.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, some way must be found by which we can provide for job security without jeopardizing the need for a high level of productivity and technological innovation. It seems to me that the fundamental link, the key to the reconciliation to this apparent dilemma, lies in training and in retraining. But in my view this in turn will never be accomplished unless the whole status of training, our attitudes here and the attitudes of the public to training are in turn completely changed and upgraded.
Traditionally training has been something which has been done in response to chronic unemployment. When a person becomes unemployed the solution has been to train him. However, training should be far more a part of the continuing process of adaptation which is a necessary part of the technological era in which we live. So training, instead of simply being something we do to assist unemployed workers, must be something we do to prevent unemployment and to enable workers to adapt to the new processes and new skills which they will be required to have.
It is this dimension, Mr. Chairman, of the resolution which to my mind is so important. There often seems to be a sort of reluctance to take preventive steps. Too often we deal with problems after the fact. For example, we deal with unemployment when unemployment arises. We are now dealing with the prospect of unemployment prior to it taking place and we are trying to pre-empt it or to prevent such an occurrence.
I think the hon. member for York East made a point into which I hope the minister will look carefully. He developed it at some length and I wish only to reiterate it. I refer to the need to bring training programs right on to the factory or shopfloor. It seems to me that far too much use is made of the approach whereby a man is taken out of his job location and put into something which passes for a school in order to train him to go back to a machine or to facilities which bear very little relationship to the equipment he learned about at the school itself.
When I was fortunate enough to work in England with a Canadian subsidiary, which is an interesting reversal, the company for

DEBATES	May 19, 1966
which I worked felt it incumbent upon them-they employed 5,000 to 6,000 workers -to provide apprenticeship training programs right in the factory itself even though they recognized from the beginning that they would never use all these people. Nevertheless it was an obligation the company assumed on their part for the good of the country.
I think that a great deal more could be done to provide training programs within factories on the shop floor in co-operation with the management of the particular industry involved. In the same light it is important that the industry involved must be prepared to disclose its long-term plans. Too often now a man is laid off without any forewarning, whereas quite frequently management has known well in advance that it will be automating a certain process and that personnel will be laid off and will therefore need retraining. Industry must be far more forthright than it has been up to now with regard to its long-term plans, and it can certainly do this without jeopardizing its competitive position in the market.
That, Mr. Chairman, is the first dimension under this resolution which I think is important, and I hope that within this dimension of training as a response to a continuing process of adaptation we will in some way discover how to work with the industries in order to get training programs out of the classroom and on to the shop floor.
The other dimension under this resolution which I think is important is the concept that payment for training must relate to payment for work and is not relative to what welfare payments might be or unemployment insurance payments. Training is an alternative to work. It is a preparation for further work, and this concept inherent in the resolution is to my mind one of the most important and enlightened concepts I have encountered in my short term in this house.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
However-and I will close on this note- one of the members opposite suggested that it was the responsibility of the minister to keep the people aware of this program; and I think that there he suggested only a halftruth. It is his responsibility and the responsibility of his department, but far more it is the responsibility of members of parliament. A good member of parliament has close and direct communication with the trade unions in his riding as well as with management
May 19, 19G6	COMMONS
and each of us in this house, it seems to me, has a compelling responsibility to make those people who are involved aware of the resolution which is being presented and the bill to follow and tell them how they can participate. It is too easy to say that it is simply the responsibility of the government to go about the country enlightening people as to what this program contains. It is equally the responsibility of members of parliament to do that job, and this applies not only to the resolution before us now but to a whole series of resolutions. I hope that hon. members who have expressed themselves so clearly in favour of this resolution will, when this measure becomes law, be just as enthusiastic about proselytizing the public and making them aware of its provisions.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, members of all parties have, as one might expect, greeted this resolution and the speech the minister made when introducing it with almost unanimous accord. As far as they go the proposals are excellent. It has been apparent for a long time from speeches made across the country and briefs presented to government by labour organizations and economists that our manpower training program has serious defects.
The Canadian Labour Congress and its affiliated unions made representations to the government about the fact that allowances paid to workers who were in theory being encouraged to avail themselves of retraining programs simply failed to provide the funds necessary to enable them to live in any kind of decency and to provide for their families. Similarly, the provision that money paid to them during training should be deducted from unemployment insurance benefits led to a situation where many workers either declined to take training programs or else failed to complete their courses. There is no means of knowing how many people failed to complete their training simply because they could not afford to continue their courses but it must have been a large number. However, hon. members can certainly greet the present program with enthusiasm even though some of us may feel it is coming several years too late.
As usual, however, instead of dealing with all the implications of this complex problem we are concerning ourselves with only two of the more important aspects. The Canadian Labour Congress, in its statement of economic policy approved at its convention in April of this year, listed a number of points which
DEBATES	5311
Vocational and Technical Training were considered to be important in regard to the question of manpower. I wish to put them on record, Mr. Chairman, because it will become obvious as I read them that we are dealing in this resolution with only two of a number of problems. Basic programs should, the congress says, include:
1.	A continuing, up-to-date research program to carry out analysis and forecasting of changes in the labour market.
2.	A nation-wide network of adult training centres to retrain men and women for new jobs requiring higher or different skills.
3.	A massive program of technical-vocational training for adolescents and pre-employment youth to prepare them for the kind of labour market they will face on leaving school.
4.	A program of financial and other assistance to workers and their families who wish to move to other parts of the country in the pursuit of employment.
5.	A program of financial assistance to maintain workers during retraining or during a transition period between jobs.
6.	A first-rate placement service.
7.	A program for the recruitment of immigrant workers, related to the Canadian labour market situation, and for their integration into the labour market.
8.	An education program to inform employers, workers and youth of the changes occurring in the labour market and the benefits to be derived from manpower programs.
The hon. member for Peterborough suggested that this last item was a job which members of parliament could do. I disagree with him completely. There are members of parliament who have close connections with trade unions. There are members who have intimate relations with employers in their areas. But there are very few who have close connections with all sections in their constituencies and who have the time or the facilities to do the job of information servicing which requires to be done. It is obvious it is the government which must do this job.
One of the severest criticisms of the national employment service on the part of both employers and employees is that they do not know what services are available from N.E.S. and that that organization in turn does not know either what the employers need or what opportunities are available. I believe that the government must not only set up a manpower program but go out and inform employers and employees alike of what the government manpower service has to offer.
A manpower training program is bound to be a failure if the government does not establish a research organization to keep in close touch with employers and employees
5312	COMMONS
Vocational and Technical Training and study employment trends as they develop. Its staff, including highly skilled sociologists, economists and statisticians, must keep in touch with the Department of Industry as well as with individual industrial organizations so that it is in a position to know what employers are likely to need in the way of manpower in the period of one to five years ahead. Unless this is done the manpower program which the government is announcing through this resolution will be to a large extent wasted.
The program now provides for the payment of up to $90 per week to workers who are being trained.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Under this provision workers can afford to take the training without losing money and without their families being put in a position in which they are not able to meet their basic financial needs. But along with this program of training grants the government must reconsider and change its policy with regard to moving allowances. The program we now have for making loans to workers is simply not good enough.
I trust, as a result of the manpower training program which the government has initiated and the training grants which the minister announced, that a large number of workers will take this opportunity to acquire new and necessary skills. But it will be of little use to an unemployed coal miner on Cape Breton Island if after taking such a course the cost of moving himself, his family and furniture to another job runs to $1,000 or $2,000. A loan of $2,000 repayable in two years at 6 per cent interest is a substantial debt for any worker who has been unemployed.
I suggest that in addition to the government's present proposal it change the system of making loans to workers to a system of making grants so that if there is no work in their own areas they can move to areas where there are jobs. Such a program has been in effect in most of the countries of western and northern Europe for many years. It has been proposed in this country on a number of occasions by labour unions. It has proven itself worth while in countries much smaller than ours, countries in which it is much cheaper to move to a new job than in a country like Canada which stretches for thousands of miles from coast to coast.

DEBATES	May 19, 1966
I suggest that the government give serious consideration to paying the cost of moving workers to new jobs. It should also give serious consideration to emphasizing the necessity for on-the-job training. It should stress to industry and unions the necessity for such training and should participate financially itself.
The largest union in Canada, the United Steelworkers of America, conducted a survey of plants it had organized and with which it had contracts to see what these plants were doing in the way of on-the-job training, and what it found is indeed a sad commentary on what is being done in this country. A report submitted by Mr. Michael Fenwick of the United Steelworkers to a conference sponsored by the Canadian Labour Congress in Ottawa last year, at which the minister also spoke, stated:
Of the 488 plants, mines and mills under union agreement in 113 communities in the five provinces, 450 returned completed survey forms. Only 1,404 of the 97,604 workers in these industries were receiving any training. Four of five plants and mines covered by the survey do not train any apprentices. More than two-thirds do not provide any on-the-job training to prevent workers from becoming obsolete and unemployed.
Farther on he reported:
The survey showed that the basic steel, fabricating, aluminum and mining companies under contract to the union had only 505 apprentices. Another 899 workers were receiving on-the-job training. Metal mining is one industry which is experiencing a shortage of skilled men. Its response to this shortage is to seek experienced mine workmen from Europe and other foreign labour markets rather than train Canadians.
Canadian industry, which is faced with a tremendous shortage of skilled workers and is going through an unprecedented period of prosperity and profits, needs to be convinced that it has a social responsibility to play its part in the training of skilled workers. The government ought to take a lead in convening joint industry and labour conferences across the country at which the necessity for on-the-job training would be emphasized.
I realize there are constitutional difficulties. I realize that education is a provincial responsibility, but I do not believe any provincial government would refuse to co-operate with the federal government and with the department of manpower when it is established in urging upon industry and labour that they should play an aggressive part in helping Canada get the skilled and trained manpower which is required.
May 19, 1966

I want to close by quoting a couple of paragraphs from a report made by Mr. Larry Sefton, director of district No. 6 of the United Steelworkers of America, on May 13, 1965, to a national policy conference. In respect of this particular problem he said:
To wait for customers to come into the government store is a gesture of futile optimism. The government must send its experts into the field. It must pass the laws needed to provide for a periodic inventory of our manpower resources. It must chart a master statisiteal inventory which will provide finger-tip data as a basis for well planned action.
Above all, it must develop a positive philosophy of investment in manpower which will guarantee the full use of the skills and productivity potential of Canadian workers.
Vigorous training and upgrading programs must also be included in any effective handling of manpower policies. And provisions must be made to pay displaced workers a living wage so that they can remain in the consumer market as long as thev are unemployed.
With the exception of what is mentioned in the last sentence, none of the things which Mr. Sefton listed as required is yet being done or has yet been publicly proposed by the government.
I conclude by again commending the minister and the government for the beginning made by introducing this resolution which is the first step toward implementation of the basic requirements of a meaningful manpower policy. Before this session ends I hope the minister will also deal with the problems he has not yet dealt with but which are of as much importance as the two he outlined in his speech the other day. If he does not, then, as so often happens in this country, we will have solved two problems having to do with manpower and created six or eight other problems just as serious as the ones we have solved.

Mr. Chairman, I want to seize this opportunity to support the resolution. In my opinion, what the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Marchand) proposes today is intended to improve the technical and vocational training program for the unemployed and for persons displaced by technological changes in industry and the services.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that this measure comes after an act passed and applied some years ago. An improvement of the said act was needed and it is timely because it is wanted by all our people.
I am of the opinion that up to now the present act providing for the training of workers, unemployed and persons displaced by the new industrial processes did not yield the expected results.
Industrial development is essential but the only sound economic system is the one which will produce and distribute the maximum amount of goods and services with a minimum amount of work and effort. The objective of any modern democratic government is to bring machinery under control and to free humanity, but at the present time, it is the
5314	COMMONS
Vocational and Technical Training machines which are reducing humanity to slavery because of a fundamentally wrong financial system.
One must not blame industry or private enterprise for wanting to improve their services and to cut down production costs, because all Canadians will benefit from such measures. But since our financial system has not recognized that, the government must face crises and problems of widespread unemployment, poverty and destitution.
The government has just realized that our labour force is ill-prepared to face such a development in our industries and it declares itself ready to cope with the crisis which has been existing for a few years already, by making more attractive the training methods of displaced workers and the unemployed.
However, in spite of all the combined goodwill of governments, employers and trainees,
I doubt that we will achieve full employment because our industries produce at an increasingly rapid pace with a decreasing number of people.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the trustee board of the Presbyterian Church in Canada was incorporated by chapter 64, Statutes of Canada, 1939, for the purpose of acquiring, taking and holding and dealing with real and personal property of the church.
There has been only one amendment which is found in the Statutes of Canada, 1962-63, chapter 23. It widened the field of investment to include investments in which a Canadian insurance company might invest and granted power to establish plans for gratuities, pensions, superannuation, etc., for ministers or former ministers of the Presbyterian Church in Canada. Section 23 was also added clarifying the refernces in the act to the board of administration or the administrative council.
At the present time the trustee board consists of seven members, being the number established under the act of incorporation. Because of the increasing work of the board it is desired to make provision for enlarging the number of members to a maximum of 15 and, until otherwise determined by the general assembly of the church the board shall consist of nine members.
While not legally obligated to do so, it has been the practice to appoint the chairman of the administrative council and the treasurer of the church to the board. Because of the nature of their offices it is desired to make these appointments mandatory. However, it is possible that the office of the treasurer of the church might at some future time become a 23033-337
Private Bills
permanent paid position or, alternatively, might cease to exist under that name. In either of these two events it is desired to appoint the person holding the position of chairman of the finance committee of the administrative council, by whatever name the position is called, to the board in place of the treasurer. Here again such an appointment would only be effective if that position was not a paid position.
At the present time the board invests separately all trusts and funds under its administration. Because of the substantial increase in income which can be obtained by so doing, it is desired to consolidate those of the church's investments which it is not prohibited from consolidating by the terms of the instruments creating them.
Because of the experience, knowledge and facilities available to them but not readily available to the board, it is also desired to give the board power to employ professional advisers to assist in making these investments. The board would of course at all times retain an overriding control over the activities of such professional advisers.
Because of the amendments proposed with respect to the membership and tenure of office of the board it is desired to substitute a new section for the old section 21 in order to bring the language of that section into line with the amendments. In addition, as the general assembly has recently approved a new code of regulations it is felt that reference to these should be made in the present amendments.
As the general assembly meets once a year only, and as there often arise decisions relating to the trustee board's work requiring implementation between meetings of the general assembly, it is considered essential that the general assembly be authorized to delegate its power of approval to the administrative council or to the executive thereof. The general assembly will have the power to revoke any such delegation at any time. Those are the proposed amendments, Mr. Speaker.

Today we are being asked as a group of politicians to pass judgment upon the worthiness and value of the general assembly of the Presbyterian Church and its considered opinion that there should be a certain number of appointed or elected officers. We are being asked to make a determination whether it is correct for the Presbyterian Church to deal in a certain manner with its moneys. I submit, first, that it should not be the function of politicians to make these decisions and, second, I do not think we are competent to do so in any event.
Some years ago the decision was made that there should be a separation of church and state but in a sense we are now in a very slight way putting church and state back together. I am quite sure that if the Presbyterian Church in Canada met to consider the rules by which Parliament would operate we would become rather incensed about it, even though they might do a much better job than we have. I am sure we would object to an outside body making determinations about who should be our officers or the manner in which we should function. Yet this is what is being asked of us now in so far as the internal functions of the Presbyterian Church of Canada are concerned. I for one do not particularly want to make that decision because I do not think it is any of my business and I do not think it is the business of any other person in parliament or any other part of parliament to make decisions of this nature.
This leads me to another point. I would appreciate it very much, and I am sure others

would, if the Presbyterian Church would find some other way of having its internal affairs dealt with so that they will be masters in their own house and do not have to ask the parliament of Canada to endorse their legitimate requirements for their own housekeeping purposes.
Let us look at the explanatory notes of the bill. One of the principal points contained within the bill is "to enable the general assembly to fix the membership of the trustee board at from seven to 15 members, with the membership fixed at nine until the general assembly otherwise determines." But unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, this is the way the system works. The act incorporating the Trustee Board of the Presbyterian Church in Canada initially came into being, if I understand correctly, in 1939 by way of a private bill piloted through the parliament of Canada. Because this system was followed at that time the only way in which changes can now be made is by the system and process of private bills.
I wish to take this opportunity to depart a little from the intimate point relating to the bill concerning the Presbyterian Church in Canada to speak in a little broader context. I wish to heavens the government of Canada, which is the body that has control over the order paper and has the authority to deal properly and effectively with the progress of public bills if it wants to do so, would heed the request I am now making not only on my own behalf but on behalf of a great many members of the house. It is that some general law should be passed permitting the incorporation of groups such as this in a more private way than by the parliament of Canada.
In the province of British Columbia, for instance, we have a Societies Act. That act allows organizations and groups to organize themselves in somewhat the same way as a limited liability company. They simply go through the process of filling out an application form and presenting it to the appropriate government body. Upon the application being approved they receive letters of incorporation in respect of the name by which the society or group wishes to be known. I believe this system should exist here. If the government would do that I am sure it would not find any

Mr. Speaker, may I first express my real appreciation for the courtesy of hon. members in making the arrangement by unanimous consent at the beginning of private members' hour to allow this bill to come forward in the way it has. I, the parliamentary agent, and the members of the company appreciate very much the courtesy of the house in this regard.
In closing the debate, having been unable to open it, I should like to say a few words about the bill and to answer the questions raised by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett). As he stated, the purpose of the bill is to change the name of the Pacific Coast Fire Insurance Company to The Century Insurance Company of Canada and, in French, La Compagnie d'Assurance Century du Canada, and to provide for an increase in the capitalization of the company from $1 million to $2 million.
Private Bills
The Pacific Coast Fire Insurance Company was originally incorporated as a provincial company under the laws of B.C. in 1890. In 1908 it applied to parliament and received federal incorporation. Since 1928 it has belonged to what is well known in the industry as The Century Group of insurance companies, which has its head office in England.
The head office of the Pacific Coast Fire Insurance Company is located in Vancouver, B.C., and it presently carries on business in every province of Canada except P.E.I. and writes contracts of insurance in the United Kingdom and the United States.
Dealing with the reason for the change of name, the Pacific Coast Fire Insurance Company, which is part of the Century group, is owned by the Century Insurance Trust Company of England, which again is owned by the Friends Provident and Century Life office. This is the Century group of companies which operates in Vancouver, and the reason for the change of name of the Pacific Coast Fire Insurance Company to the Century Insurance Company of Canada is a matter of internal reorganization by which the company, under the new name, will emphasize the Century Insurance Company name. It will become the central company in the Canadian operations so that it will be the Canadian company, under the name "Century", which will be the principal company in the Century group of companies.
In answer to the question posed by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, the increase in capitalization from $1 million to $2 million is simply for the purpose of providing funds for further expansion within the group, and it is not proposed that any shares authorized by the increase in capitalization will be sold to the public. The change of name and the increase in capitalization really arise from internal reorganization.
In conclusion I would like to say that I agree with the remarks made by hon. members on the other side that it is a waste of parliament's time to have bills such as this, seeking changes in name and capitalization, come before it because members of parliament are far too busy considering other things. I completely endorse the remarks made by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) and the hon. member for Timis-kaming (Mr. Peters) that the government and the house leaders of all parties should get
May 19, 1966

Vocational and Technical Training together to discover some easier way to deal with these private bills.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to take part in the discussion on the resolution, but would like to preface my remarks by a statement with regard to the comments just made by the hon. member for Grey-Bruce and the hon. member for Skeena. As most of you are aware, I am a non-smoker. I have made the suggestion in the House of Commons before that we should allow smoking, because if we did we would have a larger attendance. I agree with the hon. member for Grey-Bruce that those behind the curtains should be counted as part of the quorum. I am speaking objectively on the matter because it does not interest me whether hon. members are behind the curtains or not; the fact is that I abstain from smoking.
I wish to comment on this resolution now before the committee, and the angle that caught my eye is that part which suggests that it is expedient to introduce a measure respecting allowances to persons being trained under technical and vocational training programs. We should pass this resolution and the bill which will follow, but I think the field being offered assistance for retraining should be widened.
In this regard I should like to draw the minister's attention to the introduction in the province of Ontario of a new type of nursing education now known as the Quo Vadis School of Nursing. This school has recently been developed and operates on a system of training graduate and registered nurses, accepting students between the ages of 30 and 50. Practically all these students are married, and some are widowed. They have reached the stage in life where they have had as many children as they and their husbands intend to raise. By the time these wives or widows have reached age 36 or 37 the children are all in school and they are left alone at home during the day.
It would be impossible to maintain the hospitals in the Dominion of Canada if it were not for the presence of married women who have been willing to return to the nursing profession. I am sure there can be no argument with the flat statement that 60 per cent of the nurses on the floors of Canadian hospitals today are married women.
No one interested in hospital work in the Dominion of Canada does not thank God for the willingness of these trained nurses who return to hospitals, even though they may be married and have children. Most of them have to make arrangements for the care of


their children while they are working, and in fact one hospital in Toronto, which requires a fair sized nursing staff, operates a nursery in the hospital to look after the children of the nurses who work there during the day.
I draw attention to nursing schools deliberately because of the underlying basis upon which some of these schools are operating. The one to which I have referred has the wholehearted support of the Ontario Department of Health because it operates on the basis of training married women from approximately nine o'clock in the morning to 4.30 in the afternoon from Monday to Friday. In view of the fact that many of them have families to look after, these hours are ideal because they can return home in time to prepare the evening meal, and can be at home on Saturdays and Sundays.

More and more of our registered nurses are being trained under provisions of the Department of Education rather than the Department of Health. I stand here at this time asking the minister whether he will broaden the scope of this assistance provision to include the retraining of housewives. I read with close attention the remarks of the minister yesterday when he introduced this resolution, and I found it interesting, when you consider that I am talking about the retraining of housewives as registered nurses, that his remarks were heavily related to unemployed people who need retraining. I do not think there is any man in the house, or lady for that matter, who is going to suggest that
May 19. 1966	COMMONS
housewives are unemployed. However, if we are willing to spend money to retrain unemployed individuals in order that they can change their occupations or, as the minister said in one of his statements, so they can change their status in the labour market, surely we should be willing to consider assistance to housewives who are willing to pursue a nursing career, even though they may be 36, 37 or even 50 years of age.
At the present time the Quo Vadis School of Nursing limits its enrolment to 40 students a year, I believe. This school has been in existence for two years and has an application list for enrolment in the neighbourhood of 200. To the amazement of this school's administration, these applications come from all parts of Canada. I think I can speak knowingly in this regard when I say that the Ontario Department of Health felt that the applications would be received largely from metropolitan Toronto, in order that the students would be able to return to their homes after the day's class. I should have believed this to be true. But when the Quo Vadis School of Nursing received widespread publicity, applications came in from as far away as Vancouver from girls who were willing to look after their own board and room, because they wanted to change their occupations from stenographers and computer operators, even though they had reached age 35, 36 or over. These girls were willing, as I have said, to look after their own living expenses for a two or three-year period. This course to which I have referred is a two-year course, the third year being a paid internship year. The Quo Vadis School of Nursing is now in its second year of operation and will be graduating its first class of nurses this spring.
I should like to ask the minister whether he will seriously consider enlarging the scope of this training program to take in nursing education so that housewives can train at institutions such as I have mentioned-Beal Technical School, Weston Collegiate and Vocational Institute and Ryerson Polytechnical Institute, where the Department of Education is supporting a three-year graduate nurse course.
The shortage of trained nurses in Canada has been a problem for many years. Many people oppose the suggestion that nurses should be trained under the auspices of the Department of Education because they believe they should be trained under the auspices of the Department of Health. If a magazine is printed in New York city and sent to a subscriber in San Francisco it may cross eight postal zones in the United States, and the advertising content of the publication pays an increased postage rate depending on the distance which the magazine or newspaper travels. This is nothing but a fair imposition, and this practice should be adopted in Canada.
A zone rate of postage has been advocated in respect of periodicals in Canada for more than 40 years, to my personal knowledge. Why should a publisher of a magazine in

Toronto, be able to mail his publication to Victoria at a rate which is exactly the same as he would pay were he mailing it to Oakville, six miles away? Why should a publisher in Montreal be able to send his periodical to a city in Alberta at the same price he would pay to send it to Lachute?
The government controls the Canadian National Railways. If a customer ships anything by freight on the C.N.R. he pays according to the mileage traversed. If he sends anything by express he pays according to the mileage. If he sends a telegram through the C.N.R. system he pays in accordance with the distance the telegram goes. When a passenger travels on a plane belonging to Air Canada, which is a crown corporation, he pays according to the distance he flies. If he is shipping anything by air freight or air express, again he pays in accordance with the distance his goods are to be moved. People using the telephone system pay according to the distance over which they call. If hon. members are going through certain of our provinces where a government telephone service is in operation they will find that the provincial governments have rates which vary according to the distance called.
It is an established fact that the further you travel the more you pay-the further you ship, the more you pay-except in the postal service of Canada. If you want to mail something from Toronto to Vancouver the cost is the same as if you mailed the same thing from Toronto to Newmarket.
Why cannot we introduce a zone postal system and increase the revenues from second class mail to the point at which we shall not need to tell post office employees that they cannot be given the money to which they are entitled because there is no money in the till?

First of all, I should like to say that I believe in the three years this government has been in power, considering the three bills which are now before us, it has done more with respect to collective bargaining in the civil service than any government in Canada's history. I believe these three bills provide collective bargaining, with the choice to the civil service organization of the right to strike or the right to compulsory arbitration binding on both the government and the civil service The new public service employment act and amendments to the Financial Administration Act have created an entirely new environment in which the civil service of Canada can work.
May 19, 1966



I regret, as everyone regrets, the stoppage of work by postal employees last summer. This grew out of a system that developed in Canada whereby the conditions of employment and ultimately the wages of civil servants in Canada were determined arbitrarily. It was a wrong system whereby you had arbitration by the Civil Service Commission before you had consultation between the employers and employees. I suggest that the new acts which are presently before this parliament will entirely correct this situation. If the hon. member for Winnipeg North will look at this new legislation carefully he will find there is provision whereby the conditions of employment of people throughout the whole civil service of Canada will be governed, not department by department, but in another way through the collective bargaining process. I think this is a great step forward. It is one of the most progressive steps that has ever been taken in employee-employer relations in Canada.
My hon. friend has spoken about the difficulties that the employees in the Post Office Department have had. I sympathize with their difficulties, and I sympathized with them during the last work stoppage last year. I think this government acted completely responsibly, based on the system within which the government had to operate as a result of legislation passed by this parliament. In three brief years we have taken the steps necessary to correct this situation. I think the Postmaster General has reacted toward the postal employees very sympathetically. However, the real protection for the postal employees and for all civil servants, lies in the legislation which is presently before this house, the collective bargaining legislation, the public service employment act and the Financial Administration Act.
I think the difficulties which were raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North will be taken care of by this legislation. It seems to me that when he gets up and starts crying at this point, when the government has introduced legislation to correct these difficulties, it is like somebody standing up now and saying that some government did something which was improper back in 1918 or 1916. I believe this government has taken every responsible step toward correcting the inequities and improprieties in dealing with the civil service in Canada. We have introduced these measures on a completely impartial

basis. The bills can be considered and amended impartially by all the members of the house. When they pass this House of Commons we will have the best civil service legislation, and the employees of the government of Canada will have become public servants and will be in a position second to none in the world.

Mr. Chairman, before continuing with my remarks I should like to associate myself with other hon. members who have expressed their appreciation of the comprehensive review given by the Postmaster General of the work of his department. I should also like to express the hope
May 19, 1966

that he has a reasonably long tenure of office in this department. I am thinking, of course, of the recent succession of ministers who have held the office, which I feel has not contributed very much to the efficiency of the Post Office Department or helped the morale of the very capable civil servants who work under the minister. It has also given concern to the public of Canada at large.
Previous to the present government's taking office, when the government which was headed by the Leader of the Opposition was in office, we took under consideration changing the trend which had developed in the provision of postal premises, particularly those in western Canada. Up to that time large sums of money were allocated to the large urban centres of Canada much to the detriment of the smaller areas in the west which, even if they only had small populations, were contributing to the tax structure of the country and felt they had been neglected.
We reversed the trend which had existed over the last number of years and, under the leadership of Hon. Howard Green, former minister of public works, working in conjunction with the then postmaster general, Mr. Hamilton, and the hon. member for Ontario as minister of labour, we established an extensive program of post office construction under the winter works program, especially in these rural areas. These ranged in cost from a nominal $18,000 to $25,000, which was not too heavy a drain on the federal coffers but provided a long awaited and much needed improvement to our postal facilities, particularly in the west.
As far as I can determine at the present time, this worth-while program has been retarded or reduced in our part of the country by the present government. The indications are that only seven post offices will be constructed in Saskatchewan this year, if I have the figures aright. This is a far cry from the program originally in existence for a number of years, and it is not good enough. We have between 1,100 and 1,200 cities, towns and villages in the province of Saskatchewan, so looking at it on a proportionate basis seven post offices in this fiscal year is not sufficient.
In the period 1958 to 1963 post offices were constructed at points in my particular area such as Frobisher, Redvers, Fillmore, Carlyle and Maryfield, which are typical rural points. They have greatly appreciated the benefit of
Supply-Post Office
these new postal premises, which have certainly enhanced the postal services to the public in these areas. Estevan, the only city in my area of Saskatchewan, is very appreciative of the postal delivery service which was recently established under the present administration. I, as member of parliament, and officials from that area had received many representations for several years before a survey was made.
New postal premises should now be constructed at such places as Torquay and Creelman, to name only two in my riding. Many requests have been made by representative citizen bodies in these towns for the construction of crown buildings to provide better postal services there. May I suggest that the Postmaster General reconsider the applications from these areas and make provision in this fiscal year for the construction of the required post offices, even though he may need to include corresponding amounts in supplementary estimates.

First, I should like to congratulate the minister on his appointment. He is a young man with a bright future, and we are all looking forward to the benefits we can expect from his administration during the months ahead. I also wish to pay tribute to the staff in Ottawa and the post office staffs throughout the country, particularly to the mail carriers who deliver the rural mail and do this monotonous work day after day, often unrecognized by the people they serve. I am glad to note that this socialized branch of government is performing good service throughout the country. It is a model for the extension of this principle into other departments.
I wonder whether the minister or any of his officials has given any thought to the question of the postal department becoming a crown corporation. There are some countries where the post office is run as a crown corporation. If consideration has been given to this matter I would be interested to know what the result of these studies has been with respect to the efficiency of a crown corporation, compared with a department of government.
I wish to say a few words about post office employees. It is obvious that last year the employees had to take drastic action to bring their complaints to the attention of the government and of the public generally. I listened with great interest to the remarks made by the Minister of National Revenue

May 19. 1966
Supply-Post Office
and I was very pleased to hear oi his hopes with respect to the legislation to be introduced. We all know that the situation of the postal employees needs to be considerably improved. We hope that by the passing of the legislation providing for collective bargaining, their salaries will be increased and their working conditions made easier.
In this connection I wish to put in a word for the postmasters of small offices. Only two or three months ago my attention was called to the salaries paid to the postmaster in an isolated district in my riding. I forget the exact amount but I thought at the time it was an extremely small salary to be paid for the work which had to be done-not exactly the volume, but the hours during which the work required attention. I trust that when the position of the employees generally is being considered similar consideration will be given to postmasters, especially those in smaller post offices where there is no opportunity to earn the revenue which is earned in some of the larger offices.
A word with respect to the design of buildings. The hon. member for Athabasca referred to this subject. I have always been interested in building design. In recent years the Post Office Department has had a program for building post offices in smaller communities, and I suggest further consideration be given to the design of these post offices. They should be designed to meet the environment in which they are being built. If built on the prairies, I can well understand the California bungalow type with a flat roof; but in mountainous country a different type of design is more suitable if it is to be in harmony with the surrounding buildings. When travelling across Canada all post offices one enters in small communities should not be identical one with the other.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
Also, further consideration should be given to the installation of air conditioning in climates where it is required, particularly on account of the lint which I understand comes from the handling of mail bags.
I am a bit of a stickler so far as protocol and courtesy are concerned, and there is a great lack of both in our modern society. I believe many of our ills would be overcome if our people were trained to have good manners, but we are living in a world where good manners are almost obsolete. People push by you without saying pardon, and they even occupy your desk in this house and you have

to stand beside them for ten minutes in order to take your seat.
I am referring to the matter of flying the flag. It is becoming quite prevalent in many of the small buildings of the Department of Public Works that the flag is raised, stays up over night, and remains flying until it is tattered, at which time they send for a new one. I suggest that the minister would be well advised to issue instructions that the flag be raised at sunrise and lowered at sundown, which is the custom in our country.

They are not my
buildings.

The minister rather laughs at my suggestion, but I suggest there should be a certain amount of self-discipline within a department with respect to our flag. I was not one who voted for it, but it is our flag. I respect it, and I suggest that such a direction be sent out to the janitors of all post offices in Canada.
They are public works employees.

Then I suggest that the Minister of Public Works be tipped off.
Consideration should also be given to the scale of remuneration paid to rural mail route operators. I know in some cases where contracts, because they are difficult to perform, are fairly reasonably remunerated. But in other cases where there is considerable bidding, contractors have undertaken jobs which they cannot afford to perform. There are one or two in my riding and they deserve consideration.
The public should be informed of what a rural route contractor has undertaken to do and where he is supposed to deliver the mail. On occasions, in heavy snowstorms a contractor passes by mail boxes because he cannot get his vehicle close to them. The public along a mail route should understand what a contractor has undertaken to do. Post office patrons should be informed of the type of mailbox they should build to suit the convenience of the department and contractor.
I have known a case where a man put his mail box up in a tree, and in such an instance it is quite unfair to ask the contractor to drive some distance off to the side of the road to put mail in the box. The swing-type box is more convenient. Mail boxes should be standardized. One sees all sorts of boxes along the routes.
May IS. 1966
In Kootenay West?

I have seen some strange things happen with the Post Office Department in Kootenay West. In one small office, which is not in operation now, the postmaster used to put in his own day at the office. Then he used to hang the bag for registered mail and the bag for ordinary mail on the post office door. The bus would come along about four hours later and pick them up. Over a period of many years this went on, but nobody stole the mail because they were all so honest in the part of the country I represent. However, that is not carried on at the present time because now we have more of a floating population.
I should like to say a word about stamps. I think the stamps issued by the Post Office Department have improved throughout the years, although we still are somewhat behind Indonesia, Switzerland, and countries of that sort. I think we should continue still to do our best to keep up with some of the underdeveloped countries in Asia.
In respect of the services provided by the department in larger and smaller centres, I suggest that it might be a good idea to have some of the senior officials within the district -say for instance in British Columbia the district superintendent or senior inspector -make a point of addressing organizations such as service clubs, labour bodies or other groups concerning the work and services being undertaken by the Post Office Department. I think by doing this we would add to the understanding by the public of the work done and the services provided by the department. I have been told that in other departments the senior officials are rather reluctant to do this, because they are almost afraid of stepping into the field of policy. I think the minister who now is searching for new ideas might draw up a set of guide lines on subjects which might be covered by senior officials when they address organizations such as Rotary clubs and the like.
I am not quite clear as to what is the function of the international bureau. I see there is an item in the estimates in respect of this. Would the minister explain what Canada's relationship is to this bureau and what it undertakes. I was going to say something about air transportation, but I see time is passing and my friends to my rear are waiting impatiently hoping I will get through as soon as possible, because they wish to take part in the ten o'clock show, which probably

will not get started until 10.30. I should like the minister to explain why more second class mail cannot be carried at present by air. I am not speaking of periodicals. Why cannot more second class mail be carried by air than is being carried at the present time?
