GRAIN-PRINCE RUPERT, B.C.,-INCREASE IN ELEVATOR CAPACITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this matter of the extension of grain elevator facilities in Prince Rupert, as I have done on many occasions in the past. On one of the earlier occasions the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) made some reference to what he called the distribution of a poison pen letter in western Canada, someone was kind enough to send me a copy of

that letter and I should like to quote from it briefly. In part it states:
From the year 1962 until the present time, Hon. Alvin Hamilton, in his role as spokesman for western agriculture, has been keenly aware of the need for improved elevator space and has pressed for this needed construction with initiative and persistence.
That letter was circulated by the Conservative party and I should like to inform this house that it is not a true statement. When the hon. member for Qu'Appelle was the minister of agriculture he wrote a letter to the Prince Rupert chamber of commerce in which he flatly refused to extend grain elevator facilities in the city of Prince Rupert. That letter was written in 1963. So I wish that the Conservatives, when they distributed this information, had taken the trouble to learn the facts.
The National Farm Union presented a brief to the government not long ago and in that brief expressed their regret that the government was not going to proceed with the extension of the grain elevator at Prince Rupert. I submit that their concern over the matter of grain movement is one which others of us should also be concerned about. The Prince Rupert grain elevator, by the designation of officials in the Department of Agriculture and the Board of Grain Commissioners, has been rated as the second most efficient grain elevator in the country.
In a report dated April 12, 1962, in which it was urged that the elevator be extended, the general manager of the Canadian Government Elevators stated that a far more efficient operation could be carried out at Prince Rupert than is possible with the present l\ million bushels capacity, if the grain elevator were extended. At that time we had an average cargo shipment out of Rupert of some 500,000 or 550,000 bushels on each ship. We have had shipments even larger than that to move. Unfortunately, with the limited working capacity of the elevator being 850,000 bushels, it is just not possible to have two cargoes of grain available at the same time; as a consequence there is delay in the shipment of grain through the port of Prince Rupert. This has required, of course, the Canadian Wheat Board to place strict control upon the movement of grain into Rupert because they do not want cars sitting up on the track, unloaded, waiting for the grain to be screened and stored ready for shipment.
There is another serious problem in Rupert because of the limited facilities, and this
May 19. 1966

involves the cleaning of grain. The report of the general manager of Canadian Government Elevators deals with this matter by pointing out that it caused some delay in the loading of ships at the port and as a consequence they had to employ casual labour and overtime workers to a far greater extent than would otherwise have been necessary. In his report he intimated that in the year 1961-62 a saving of approximately $75,000 in overtime and casual payrolls could have been realized had the additional space been available.
The Conservative government when in office refused to deal with this matter, even though extended facilities were recommended by Canadian Government Elevators. The Liberal government has now taken the course of refusing to proceed with the elevator because of what it classifies as inordinately high bids on the cost of the elevator, while at the same time they are prepared to pour millions of dollars into increased construction projects such as the centre of the performing arts and Expo '67.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that before this situation deteriorates to an even worse state than it has, the government should take some definitive action and proceed with the construction of this elevator at the earliest possible moment.

CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-REQUEST FOR TEXTBOOKS IN FRENCH LANGUAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, further to the question I put to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) concerning bilingualism at the C.N.R., which the Chair ruled out of order, I now want to ask the minister, or his representative, if he is aware that at the C.N.R. bilingualism is trampled under foot.
The best proof I can give of this, is the letter, dated May 11, 1966, from the president of the C.N.R. signed by R. T. Vaughan.
I had written to him about Mr. Blackburn who complained about having failed his signalling examination because he was a French-Canadian unilingual. Mr. Vaughan wrote the following letter in reply, barely two days ago.
He answered me:
Some time ago, you have exchanged correspondence with Mr. Gordon about Mr. Jean Marc Blackburn. The latter was complaining that he had been fired by the C.N.R. because he was not sufficiently conversant with the English language.
I swear to you, Mr. Speaker, that if the same requirements were applied to all English speaking people who are unilingual in the civil service, only about 18 per cent of the personnel would remain throughout Canada.
Is that total bilingualism such as was preached all through the election campaign by the Liberal party? One set of laws for French speaking Canadians, another for English speaking Canadians; one law for the rich, another for the poor. Such, too, is the reason for all our differences since 1867, to save the remains of confederation the meaning of which a certain English speaking group has to this day failed to grasp fully.
French Canadians are required to study with English text books in order to survive and if a voice is raised in protest, the other group seems shocked and asks: What do those French Canadians want?
May 19, 1966

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
We are constantly treated with contempt and when we refuse to knuckle under any longer, obstacles are raised to the advancement of our people.
For instance, on the Saguenay-Lake St. John train that plies between Dolbeau and Chicoutimi, we have been asking the government for four years now, to have French speaking personnel on a train serving a population about 98 per cent French speaking. I take that train every Friday and on numerous occasions, I have noted that the employees spoke only English and I even had to act as interpreter on the train because the employees were unilingual.
Well, believe it or not, that is taking place on trains which serve a population which is 98 per cent French Canadian.
I would like to see the reaction of those good westerners if anyone ever tried to put on their trains a French Canadian who did not speak a single word of English. And some people talk about the province of Quebec being revolutionary minded.
Who knows but that the makers of that revolution are some English speaking people who have never understood and still do not want to understand anything about the discrimination which we are facing today.
Mr. Vaughan says very candidly in his letter that the examiner, Mr. Bissonnette, is perfectly bilingual, whereas all the books used for the courses are in English only.
They put handcuffs on us and say: Be happy, at least your jailer speaks your language.
If that is what the government calls cooperative federalism, you may be sure that we will fight it to the death.
Mr. Vaughan also says in his letter that Mr. Tardif wrote in French to Mr. Blackburn to inform him that his services were no longer required for signalling.
Well, Mr. Speaker, when it comes to telling a French Canadian: step aside and make room for someone else, then another French Canadian is used to do the work.
At least, Mr. Vaughan is sincere when he writes me:
With regard to the signalling courses, I must tell you that they are the same throughout the network and that the manuals are in English only.
And Mr. Vaughan concludes:
Therefore, we would have to translate not only the courses, hut also the changes resulting from technological progress.

What is the government waiting for to do something? Another centennial? For a hundred years, we have been told: "it is necessary", "it would be better"; promises are made from one election to the next, but nothing is ever done. And what reason is given for that? Listen to Mr. Vaughan himself:
Because of the high cost of such an undertaking and also because of the lack of competent translators, we are unable to do it for the time being.
Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, a vice president of the Canadian National Railways who dares to write those lines about the high cost of the translation work, when the president of the C.N.R. is paid $75,000 a year, over and above a special train that is provided to him for his travelling. When I think, Mr. Speaker, that they come and speak about the cost of translation. Well, in all that, the vice-president brings forward the argument of the high cost of translation as concerns respect for confederation. And what is more-

Mr. Speaker, we have been assured in the discussions with the officials of the Canadian National Railways that the gentleman referred to in this letter was not dismissed because he was unable to speak English, but rather that he simply did not qualify for the position. He was offered an alternative position which he has accepted.
The signalling courses given by the C.N.R. are conducted along the same lines as similar engineering courses offered by l'Ecole Polytechnique in Montreal. The course is given in both English and French, using however, an English language manual. As is the case at many educational institutions in Quebec, while the text of the manual is in English, instruction is given in French.
This is not to say that the technical manuals are not available in French from the C.N.R. or that the company is not progressing in its bilingualism policy. Only today the company issued a press release, and if the hon. member will permit me I should like to quote from the release.
Canadian National is intensifying its efforts in developing a comprehensive and practical business and technical railway terminology In the French language adapted to North American conditions ...
May 19, 1966

The company's translation bureau will be expanded with the addition of a terminology section and which hereafter will be known as "Linguistic Services". Its function will be to gather material and to make it easily available to the employees and to the customers of the railway.
[DOT] (10:40 p.m.)
"The lack of an adequate and easily accessible French language railway terminology adapted to North American realities is becoming a serious handicap especially when long range goals are considered", said Mr. Gordon.
"We have encountered this problem in our extensive customer and community relations and the need is felt daily in such vital activities as employee training, and employee communications. Consequently the objective of linguistic services will be to facilitate and encourage the use of French as well as English as a working language for both oral and written communications within the Canadian National system."
Linguistic services will report to the vice president and secretary of the company, Mr. R. T. Vaughan and will be headed by Frederic Phaneuf until now special assistant to the vice president St. Lawrence region.
Mr. Phaneuf is well known in public relations and translation circles and is currently president of the Society of Translators and Interpreters of Canada.
The decision to create a Canadian National linguistic service arises from a recommendation of Canadian National permanent committee on bilingualism which is under the chairmanship of Mr. Maurice Archer, vice president research and development. Canadian National linguistic sections will work in close conjunction with similar organizations in the federal government, in the Quebec provincial government and in other provinces, where established, as well as in private industry.

UNITED NATIONS-PROPOSED JURISDICTION OVER HIGH SEAS AND OUTER SPACE
speechtext:
Before orders of the day were called today I addressed a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs asking him whether the government had under consideration a proposal which had been advanced that the United Nations be given ownership and jurisdiction over the high seas and outer space. Mr. Speaker ruled that this question was more suitable for the order paper, but since I felt it involved a matter of great national and international importance it seemed to me we should know as soon as possible whether our government had this matter under consideration and learn, if possible, what its views are.
The organization which made the report to which I referred is the commission of the United Nations Association of the United States of America. In its 17th annual report, this commission, which has been set up to promote the establishment of peace, put forward in some detail a proposal to extend the
DEBATES	5355
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion jurisdiction of the United Nations in this area. The report states that in the commission's view the United Nations should declare the title of the international community to the high seas and outer space, for six reasons.
The reasons given are as follows: to avoid conflicts between nations over these areas, to keep their resources from being wasted, to prevent their military use, to head off their contamination, to make sure all nations could benefit from their resources, and to provide the United Nations with an independent source of income. The final point refers to the resources of the high seas and I suppose at some future date outer space could be used to help provide the United Nations with an independent source of income.
This report, which was signed by 70 members, including scholars, writers, editors, union leaders and business executives, all members of the United Nations Association in the United States, has, in my view, pinpointed matters of grave concern not only to Canadians but to all the peoples of the world, and matters which are relevant to the internal problems of this country.
I make particular reference to questions related to the resources of the high seas, with which I, and other hon. members have become much involved from the viewpoint of the future of the fishing resources of Canada. The house will recall there was much discussion in this connection when the bill to extend the territorial seas and fishing zones of our country was introduced.
I think that the fact that this proposal is put forward by a responsible body in the United States, expressing a viewpoint in many ways contradictory to that which is held by the United States, particularly in relation to the fisheries negotiations currently taking place in Seattle, makes it a matter worthy of immediate consideration by this house and we should have some statement from the government on its views.
Not only are our own resources involved but also what is known as the cornerstone of our foreign policy, namely support for the United Nations. Certainly this idea is related to our involvement with the costs and maintenance of the various UN peace keeping forces.
This commission has suggested that if the United Nations could derive revenues, what we in Canada would call royalties, from leasing resources of the high seas, those funds could be used by the Secretary General for the maintenance of a peace keeping force
5356	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion enlisted directly with the United Nations. It is suggested that a force of some 2,000 men would be appropriate for this purpose, immediately available under the direction of the Secretary General of the United Nations for dispatch to trouble spots, until such time as contingents from member nations could be gathered and sent to aid it.
This proposal is one which should be of great interest not only to hon. members but to Canadians generally. It is also one that should be brought forward for formal study by the General Assembly of the United Nations, as is suggested by this commission.

Mr. Speaker, we are grateful to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) for having raised this interesting question. Twice in the course of his remarks he has stated that this proposal was put forward by a responsible body. It is important that no one be misled.
To this date the government has examined only the press accounts, but it has been clearly ascertained from these newspaper stories that the commission making this recommendation is an entirely private body, part of

the United Nations Association of the United States of America, and not a committee of the United Nations organization.
[DOT] (10:50 p.m.)
It is hoped that eventually we shall be able to give careful consideration to its suggestions when we see a first-hand account of its annual report which we have yet to receive. We have noted, however, that as mentioned by the hon. member one of these suggestions is United Nations ownership of both the high seas and outer space. While it is true that the General Assembly has passed resolutions treating outer space in much the same manner as the high seas, for instance in declaring that it was not subject to national appropriation, a proposal that ownership of outer space and the high seas should be vested in the United Nations obviously would have far reaching legal implications and consequently would require very thorough study.
